articles.fullContent: Linux のデスクトップを、Windows XP のシェルで。 日本語 · English Important個人の実験的なプロジェクトです。 日常の作業環境として使えるほど完成してはいません。 動作を確かめているのは、新しくインストールした Debian 13 に導入スクリプトで入れた場合だけです。 すでに使っている環境（ほかのデスクトップ環境やディスプレイマネージャが入っているものなど）への導入は試していません。 試すときは、仮想マシンや試験用のマシンをおすすめします。 これは何？ Windows XP の explorer.exe を、パッチを当てた Wine の上で Linux のデスクトップシェルとして動かすプロジェクトです。 タスクバー、スタートメニュー、デスクトップ、フォルダウィンドウは XP 本物のものです。Linux のアプリも、XP の枠とタスクバーで扱えます。 Microsoft のファイルは同梱していません。お手元の XP の ISO から、必要なファイルだけを取り出して使います。 XP の ISO が無い方は、XP のシェルの代わりに ReactOS のシェル（Windows 2000 風のクラシックの見た目）でも 試せます。ReactOS は自由なソフトウェアなので、導入スクリプトが公式のリリースから取得します（docs/reactos.md）。 Windows 7 の ISO があれば、Windows 7 のシェル（Windows 7 ベーシックの見た目）でも試せます。まだ実験的な試作です（docs/windows7.md）。 できること XP のシェル: Luna（またはクラシック）のタスクバー、スタートメニュー、デスクトップ、マイ コンピュータ、フォルダウィンドウ。 Linux アプリとの統合: Linux のウィンドウに XP の枠が付き、タスクバー、Alt+Tab、最小化・最大化が XP と同じように動きます。 Linux のアプリは「すべてのプログラム」に並びます。 通知領域: Linux のトレイアイコン（StatusNotifierItem と XEmbed）が XP の通知領域に出ます。 XP 自身のネットワーク・バッテリー・音量のアイコンと、そのフライアウト（音量、電源メーター、ワイヤレス ネットワーク接続の状態）も 出ます。NetworkManager と PipeWire / PulseAudio の状態から作ります（AshesTom さんのフォークの XP Explorer から）。 ワイヤレス ネットワークの一覧から、初めてのネットワークにも XP のネットワーク キーの画面で接続できます。メニューや画面の文字は ISO の XP のファイルから読みます。 XP Explorer からの追加: フォルダの左のタスク ペイン、画面のプロパティ（Windows XP とクラシックのテーマ、スタイルと配色。 配色は ISO の HIVEDEF.INF と themeui.dll から作ります）、画像の縮小版とプレビュー、XP のサウンド（起動、ログオン、ログオフも）、 ネットワーク接続、Internet Explorer 6、Windows Media Player 9、スタートメニューの左の列（インターネット、電子メール、 よく使うプログラム）。どれもお手元の ISO のファイルで動きます（prefix/extras.py）。 キーボードの配列: 最初は Linux のシステムの配列（localectl）です。コントロール パネルの「地域と言語のオプション」→ 「言語」→「詳細」（XP 自身のもの）で入力言語を足したり既定を変えたりすると、セッションの配列（Wayland では labwc、 X11 では setxkbmap）がすぐに従います。2 つ以上なら XP と同じ左 Alt+Shift で切り替わります（session/keyboard.py）。 日本語入力: fcitx5 + Mozc です。Ctrl+Space（または全角/半角）で切り替えます。GTK、Qt、Wine のアプリで使えます。 日本語版と英語版の XP: どちらの ISO でも動きます。言語は ISO から自動で判断し、字体（英語版は Tahoma など）、 ロケール、ようこそ画面をその XP に合わせます（英語版では日本語入力は設定しません）。 Windows のアプリ: WoW64 の Wine 11.0 で、32bit と 64bit のアプリが動きます。端末で wine setup.exe と打つと、 インストーラーが作るショートカットは XP のスタートメニューに入ります。 XP のようこそ画面: LightDM の greeter として、XP のようこそ画面とログオフの画面を出せます（任意）。 シェルが起動するまでは XP と同じ大きな「ようこそ」の画面を出します。 XP のキー操作: Windows キー、Ctrl+Esc、Win+R、Win+E が使えます。 クイック起動: タスクバーの右クリック →「ツール バー」→「クイック起動」で出せます（XP と ReactOS。Windows 7 は実機と同じく 「新規ツール バー」でクイック起動のフォルダを選びます）。スタートメニューから Linux のアプリのショートカットも置けます。 「デスクトップの表示」も実機と同じく、もう一度押すと窓が元に戻ります。 画面の拡大（DPI）: XP と同じ「DPI 設定」で、文字や部品を大きくできます（96・120・144 など）。 落ちても戻れる: XP のシェルが繰り返し落ちると、Wine 標準の explorer と xterm に切り替わります。 Wayland のセッション（任意・X11 のセッション以上に実験的）: X11 のウィンドウマネージャーの代わりに、パッチを当てた labwc で 動かすセッションです（XP、ReactOS、Windows 7 のシェル）。モニターごとの倍率や 125%・150% などの倍率が使え、シェルはぼけずに描かれます。 Wayland のアプリにもシェルの枠が付きます。作ったばかりで、確かめた範囲は X11 のセッションより狭く、既知の制限もあります（docs/wayland.md）。 ふだん試すなら X11 のセッションをおすすめします。 ReactOS のシェル（任意）: XP の ISO の代わりに ReactOS 0.4.16 の explorer で動かすセッションです。日本語と英語に対応します。 XP のシェルと並べて入れられます。 Windows 7 のシェル（任意・実験的）: Windows 7 SP1 x64 の explorer で動かすセッションです（Windows 7 ベーシックの見た目。 Aero のガラスはまだありません）。スタートメニュー、タスクバー、通知領域、フォルダの窓が動き、Linux のアプリもアプリごとに タスクバーにまとまります。確かめたのは日本語版と、その文字を英語の言語パックのものに入れ替えた英語版です。 試してみる Windows XP Professional SP3（x86）の ISO（日本語版か英語版）をご自身で用意してください。 新しくインストールした Debian 13 に、ログインして使う利用者として入り、次を実行します。 git clone https://github.com/mikuta0407/win4wine.git ~/win4wine cd ~/win4wine scripts/setup.sh --media /path/to/WindowsXPSP3.iso --greeter 再起動すると、XP のようこそ画面からそのまま XP のシェルに入ります。 XP の ISO が無いときは、ReactOS のシェルで試せます（ISO は要りません）。 scripts/setup.sh --shell reactos --lang ja # 英語なら --lang en ログイン画面でセッション「ReactOS Shell (Wine, X11)」を選びます。 Windows 7 のシェル（実験的）は、Windows 7 SP1 x64 の ISO から作ります。 scripts/setup.sh --shell win7 --media /path/to/Windows7SP1x64.iso ログイン画面でセッション「Windows 7 Shell (Wine, X11)」を選びます。 詳しい手順とオプションは 🔗 導入手順（INSTALL.md） にあります。Wine をソースからビルドするので、4 コアで 1 時間半ほどかかります。 テーマ（XP articles.title: Yes, 17M lines of Lean is a lot
articles.contentSnippet:

articles.fullContent: The recent proof of the Riemann hypothesis came with a statistic attached: the proof is 17 million lines of Lean. Beyond the philosophical questions of what it means to have a proof longer than any human could comprehend, I’m left with a simpler question: is that as large as it sounds?To investigate, I hunted for collections of Lean proofs online. I found two and charted the lengths of their proofs.(All charts have a log x axis, which makes 17m lines look a lot closer to 1m and 100k than it really is.)Famous theorems in MathlibMathlib maintains a collection of famous proofs. There are over 1k but only 259 have Lean associated, which I chart here.These are all human generated, and as we can see, they come nowhere close to 17m.Every Lean package on ReservoirReservoir indexes every published Lean package, 938 of which have Lean code on GitHub. This one has a lot more data, including AI assisted proofs. We even have a few that are over 16m!:88m: Qiuzhen-CFSG/CFSG this appears to be an AI built proof that is still a work in progress.36m: CBirkbeck/LeanBridge, a project linking the LMFDB database of number theory objects to Mathlib. This isn’t really a proof: about 98% of its Lean is files generated by scripts that check the database’s numbers one by one. The hand-written part is closer to 500k lines.27m: anthropics/fermats-last-theorem is another Anthropic special: a complete proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, published on GitHub in September. Its README says “the Lean sources were produced by AI agents building on human-written open-source Lean”, including the human FLT project led by Kevin Buzzard, which is about 60k lines and still in progress. The AI version is roughly 450 times longer.So yes, 17m lines is a lot.

articles.fullContent: What is Tempo? An overview of Tempo Applications Related projects Workshop Distribution References Contact information What is Tempo? Partial evaluation is program transformation that automates a program specialization process. Tempo is a partial evaluator for C programs. It has been applied in various domains such as operating systems and networking, computer graphics, scientific computation, software engineering and domain specific languages. A first workshop on Tempo has been organized in March 1998. Tempo is now being distributed. Its documentation is available on line, as well as tutorial slides. An Overview of Tempo Tempo is a partial evaluator for C programs. It is being developed in the Compose project at IRISA / INRIA - LABRI (France). Tempo is an off-line specializer; it is divided into two phases: analysis and specialization. The input to the analysis phase consists of a program and a description of which inputs will be known during specialization and which will be unknown. Based on this knowledge, dependency analyses propagate information about known and unknown values throughout the code and produce an annotated program, indicating how each program construct should be transformed during specialization. Because C is an imperative language including pointers, the analysis phase performs alias and side-effect analyses in addition to binding-time analyses. The accuracy of these analyses is targeted towards keeping track of known values across procedures, data structures, and pointers. Following the analysis phase, the specialization phase generates a specialized program based on the annotated program and the values of the known inputs. Tempo can specialize programs at compile time (i.e., source-to-source tranformation) as well as run time (i.e., run-time binary code generation). For more details, please consider reading some of our papers, most of which are available at the following URL: papers. Program Analysis As a first step, the user provides a program and specifies what arguments (including global variables) are static. For example, the user provides the following code for a miniprintf function, and specifies in this way that the first argument is static whereas the second is dynamic: miniprintf(S,D). miniprintf(char fmt[], int val[]) { int i = 0; while( *fmt != '\0' ) { if( *fmt != '%' ) putchar(*fmt); else switch(*++fmt) { case 'd' : putint(val[i++]); break; case '%' : putchar('%'); break; default : prterror(*fmt); break; } fmt++; } } From this Tempo produces a program file with analysis annotations. These annotations can be visualized using colors that highlight the propagation of the known/unknown information throughout the program. /* LEGEND: STATIC DYNAMIC */ miniprintf(char fmt[], int val[]) { int i = 0; while( *fmt != '\0' ) { if( *fmt != '%' ) putchar(*fmt); else switch(*++fmt) { case 'd' : putint(val[i++]); break; case '%' : putchar('%'); break; default : prterror(*fmt); break; } fmt++; } } The blue color (bold face for black and white display) represent static constructions, i.e. values that can be computed at specialization time. The red color (standard font for black and white display) is for dynamic expressions, whose value cannot be precomputed knowing only the static arguments. Basically, everything in blue (bold) will disappear after specialization; only red (standard font) parts will remain. The visualization of the analysis is very important for the user to assess the amount of specialization in the code. Furthermore, the analysis speeds up the specialization process (as opposed to on-line partial evaluators). The analysis is inter-procedural and takes into account pointer aliases and side-effects. Compile-Time Specialization When the user is satisfied with the analysis (i.e., what the user expects to specialize indeed appears as static), actual specialization values must be provided. articles.fullContent: Run macOS userspace on Linux by loading the macOS kernel into it. xnulinux builds XNU, the open-source kernel of macOS, from Apple's published sources and runs it as a loadable kernel module (xnu.ko) inside an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel. The hosted XNU drives the CPU and MMU directly, so macOS processes run natively next to Linux processes on the same CPUs, with no hypervisor between them. Linux lends XNU its memory, timers, files, network and GPU through a small interface module (fki.ko). With a stock Ubuntu kernel, insmod xnu.ko boots a macOS 27 system disk made by Apple's own installer to the desktop: loginwindow, WindowServer, Dock, Finder, Safari and Chrome. One system, two userspaces. Left: a Terminal in the hosted macOS 27.2.1 (sw_vers, the Darwin kernel, launchd, WindowServer, Dock and Finder running). Right: from that macOS, an SSH session into the Linux it runs inside (Ubuntu, Linux 7.0, the xnu and fki modules loaded, and the insmod xnu.ko process the macOS kernel runs in). Straight from the hosted framebuffer, 1280×800. The hosted desktop at the end of a 30-minute stress run, rendered on the CPU (no GPU bridge). Safari in the hosted macOS: Wikipedia's article on XNU, kernel.org and the Linux repository on GitHub, over the hosted system's network link through Linux, with the GPU bridge on (GPU=auto). How it works macOS processes (launchd, WindowServer, Safari...) Linux processes (systemd, sshd, xnudrmd...) ────────────────────────────────────────────────── ──────────────────────────────────────────── XNU (source-built, LINUX64 machine layer, kexts) │ ↕ linux64 host calls (xnu-patches/include/linux64_abi.h) xnu.ko (APSL side: loads and runs the kernel collection) ↕ FKI, the foreign kernel interface (fki_*) fki.ko (GPL side: CPUs, memory, faults, IPIs, files, network, host calls) Linux kernel (stock distro kernel, 4K pages, PAC) CPUs: each hosted CPU is a Linux kernel thread pinned to a Linux CPU. XNU runs on it until it calls the host (idle, I/O, a timer); Linux keeps its own exception vectors, and fki.ko forwards the faults and user exceptions of XNU code to XNU's handlers. Memory: XNU gets one physically contiguous block from Linux (CMA) and manages it with its own pmap; XNU and Linux share the user half of the address space layout (4K pages). Devices: kexts in kexts/ give macOS a disk (a file on the Linux side), a display (a framebuffer Linux reads), a keyboard and pointer, an Ethernet link (a Linux network interface), a keystore and a GPU bridge. GPU: Metal in the hosted macOS runs on gpu/xnu-cpu-metal (metal2vulkan over Vulkan). Vulkan reaches the Linux host's GPU through the DRM bridge (kexts/XnuDrm → host call → gpu/xnu-drm/xnudrmd → the Linux render node), using Mesa's Venus driver; without a GPU it falls back to Mesa lavapipe on the CPU. Status Working, on an Apple Silicon Mac running an arm64 Linux VM (krunkit) with 1 to 6 hosted CPUs: macOS 27.2.1 boots to the desktop with auto-login in 31–48 s (an Apple Virtualization macOS VM on the same Mac: 49 s). Apps open and quit, Spotlight and the file system work; a 30-minute stress run (40 rounds of Safari, Notes, Calculator, TextEdit, System Settings, Spotlight and a disk walk) finishes with no panic and no crash report. Runs as a systemd service: started at boot, stopped cleanly with the VM, restarted after a hosted-kernel panic, each run's log kept in /var/log/xnulinux/. The GPU bridge gives hosted apps the host GPU (Virtio-GPU Venus (Apple M5 Max)) and is enabled by default (GPU=auto) when a Linux render node is present, falling back to CPU rendering (GPU=off) otherwise. What is still a stopgap is listed in docs/production.md. Notably: the OS cryptex is merged into the system volume, AMFI is patched and SIP relaxed, and memory access is slower than a native VM (4K pages vs 16K). Requirements An arm64 Linux host with PAC (Apple Silicon M1 or later in a VM: krunkit for GPU access, or tart), 4K pages, 16 GB of RAM (8 GB of it reserved for the hosted kernel).

articles.fullContent: Evolving an iconic brand for the agentic era Today, Docker is officially launching its new brand, and I’m excited to tell you what it’s all about and why we think now is the time for change. Let’s start with the big picture. We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself. AI is creating possibilities that would have sounded like science fiction not long ago. But it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control? Or, put more simply: how do we get to a point where we can actually trust agents? That one seemingly simple yet infinitely complex question is why we’re here today, introducing you to a new Docker. A new Docker, but a familiar story. We’ve been here before Ok, not exactly here, but once upon a time, a decade or so ago, the tech industry was at a similar inflection point. Digital transformation was the term du jour, promising a new way of engaging customers and powering the global economy. There was one big constraint, though: teams needed a better way to build, ship, and run software consistently across any environment. Enter a company you might have heard of: Docker. Together with all of you, Docker built the standard trusted by millions of developers. For over a decade, developers have relied on us to make software portable, open, reproducible, and secure. Docker turned the frustration of “Well, it works on my machine!” into the assurance that “Yes, it works everywhere.” Today, of course, the challenge confronting us is new and evolving, and we all need to evolve with it. We cannot simply continue to do what we’ve always done and expect to succeed in this new era. That applies to business leaders, developers, tech companies, everyone. It certainly applies to Docker. That’s what this rebrand is about: evolving to meet the moment for our customers. What isn’t changing Let me be unequivocal: this is not about leaving Docker’s legacy or heritage behind. We’ve spent more than a decade earning your trust. This is about building on that foundation, not replacing it. The qualities you value us for aren’t changing. We’re still committed to openness and industry collaboration. We’re still, and always will be, developer-first. We’re still fanatical about simplicity, and about showing up everywhere you need us. On the product front, the containers you know and love aren’t going anywhere. Containers still play a huge role in the software development lifecycle. Developers and enterprises need solutions built specifically to isolate and govern them, so they can give those agents real autonomy without giving up control. Docker’s next chapter is about delivering exactly that: security, isolation, and governance, so we can all trust agents to do meaningful work without feeling like we’re always one step from catastrophe. articles.fullContent: We have AI at home! Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen. It's private, and the whole house can use it.With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle.OpenAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models. Add to this ballooning costs and privacy concerns, and we get a pretty good case for moving away from this 'convenient' cloud experience.That's basically where I was too. I wanted to offload certain token-heavy research, data collection, or coding tasks to an AI model without staring at usage limits all day. So, as any reasonable human being would do, I decided to set up my own local AI: a Claude and ChatGPT replacement that runs at home on my own hardware.Since this was my first attempt, my primary focus was keeping it simple and hosting it on Windows. If you're a beginner, you can follow along to get one going on your home network too.Once you have the hardware sorted, it takes about 10-15 minutes (excluding download times).The short versionInstall Unsloth Desktop, download a quantized AI model that fits your GPU's VRAM, set your context size, and turn on LAN access so everyone at home can use it.What Do You Need to Run a Local AI at Home?Not much (other than the hardware). Here's a short list:A Windows PC with a graphics card (GPU). The more video memory (VRAM) it has, the bigger the model it can run. I'm using an RTX 5090 with 32GB VRAM for this setup.Unsloth Desktop. A free app that 'serves' the AI model to you through a chat interface. Get it from Unsloth.An AI model sized to fit your GPU. We'll pick one in the next section.That's it. No terminal commands, Python environments, or subscriptions required.Which AI Model Can Your GPU Run?It depends on how much VRAM your graphics card has. As a rough guide, 8-12GB of VRAM handles smaller 9B-12B models, while 32GB comfortably runs 27B-35B models with plenty of room for long conversations.On consumer-grade hardware, we'll need smaller models. The full-size Qwen model sits at around 56GB and won't really fit on a consumer graphics card unless you're running a Mac with unified memory. That's where quantization comes in.What Is Quantization?Quantization shrinks a model by compressing weights and moving to a lower precision. You basically trade some accuracy for a model that actually fits on your GPU and runs faster.The same photo stored at 8, 4 and 2 bits per pixel. A model's weights lose detail the same way going from Q8 to Q4 to Q2.If you're wondering whether this tradeoff is worth it, well, it depends. You'll find that certain types of workloads don't really care and give similar outputs, while others may be nearly unusable.Which Model Should You Run for Your VRAM?For this guide, we'll be going with Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantization on my system with an RTX 5090. Going up a tier is an option thanks to its 32GB of VRAM, but I wanted to allow for a larger context window (how much of the conversation the model can keep in mind at once) rather than cramming in the largest model that fits.Qwen3.8-27B at each precision with a 128K context, from our VRAM calculator. At 4-bit, the model and the context fit a 32 GB card with room to spare.If you want to run a model of this caliber with excellent performance, a hilariously overpriced RTX 5090 (remember when $1,999 felt too high?) is unfortunately still not a terrible 'deal' these days. articles.fullContent: Translate Zig functions into executable Lean models and prove their behavior. Zean captures Zig's analyzed intermediate representation (AIR) and emits Lean program definitions. You write specifications and proofs in separate files, then regenerate the model when the Zig code changes. Our model is currently incomplete and translation is restricted to supported operations. For memory safety, a reusable verification library generates proof obligations from the translated program using Lean 4.35's Std.WP and vcgen. You supply contracts and loop invariants, then discharge the remaining obligations in Lean. Note: This initial release of this project was written with AI assistance mostly using GPT-6 Astra over the course of two months. It is extracted from our formal verification work for oksolc, a Solidity compiler written in Zig. Try the Ziglings memory-safety demo With Zig 0.17.1 and elan installed, run from the repository root: elan toolchain install leanprover/lean4:v4.35.0 zig build ziglings The tutorial follows two familiar Ziglings lessons: Exercise Checked property of the derived runtime kernel 038: initialize both characters Reading either gold slot is safe after both writes, without assuming initial contents 054: give a many-pointer a length Reads stay within the caller's initialized byte region and preserve memory You supply the caller contracts; reusable verification rules discharge the memory obligations. Broken variants demonstrate an uninitialized read and an invented slice extent. The command checks the proofs, requires false claims to fail, and runs the two officially corrected upstream exercises on Zig 0.17.1. The formal proofs cover the captured runtime kernels described in the tutorial. The original exercises, including their printing code, receive separate native compatibility checks. Retained captures let you run the demo without building an instrumented compiler. More demos When can one thread safely read a dispatch table that another thread is filling in? The writer sets a flag with a release store after it fills both entries. The Lean proof shows that a reader can use either entry once its acquire load sees that store. Run zig build atomic-publication to check the proof and see what goes wrong if the writer sets the flag too soon. Dispatch-table example Continue with the buffer update, or follow the copy-loop tutorial for initialization, framing and helper contracts. The verification guide explains how to apply the same machinery to another supported function. The manifest-based client captures and verifies your own function without adding a new tutorial command or changing the verifier. Its caller/helper variant uses the explicit call-stack interpreter and verifies a caller from a separately checked helper contract, with readable generated function tables. The byte-scanning client adds a loop invariant, early returns, and a helper call inside the loop. For runtime helper calls, the call-chain example shows a caller reusing checked callee contracts across actual runtime calls. The standard-library example goes beyond the tutorials: it verifies an unchanged std.mem.replaceScalar(u32) specialization, with a separately checked AIR-to-model correspondence certificate. The compatibility probes also show examples that still reject, so these results should not be read as general Zig support. Follow a small program update Start with a counter that advances without overflowing: pub export fn advance(value: u8) u8 { return if (value < 255) value + 1 else 255; } The handwritten proof establishes that, for every valid byte input x, the generated model returns min(x + 1, 255) successfully. A second theorem proves that the result never decreases and never exceeds 255. zig build counter-run zig build counter counter-run runs the working Zig examples. counter checks their native results, generated-source identities, Lean proofs, and expected proof failures. The example includes generated models from real native AIR captures

articles.fullContent: A DNS blocklist of news and current-affairs websites, for people who want a break from the news. It covers newspapers, broadcasters' news sites, news agencies, news magazines, political news and commentary, business news, local news and news aggregators, worldwide. Major and regional outlets are curated in this repository. The long tail of smaller news sites is pulled from Wikidata, filtered automatically, checked against DNS, and refreshed every week. Works with Pi-hole, AdGuard Home, uBlock Origin, AdGuard, dnsmasq, hosts files and any blocker that subscribes to a list by URL. List Sites Hostnames (hosts format) news 14,314 30,863 news-lite 6,762 15,936 Choose a list List What's in it Use it when news Everything: the curated outlets plus news sites listed on Wikidata. You want the major and regional names blocked with a list half the size, or you're editing a hosts file by hand. Both block the same major sites. news adds thousands of smaller ones. Download Each list comes in five formats. Use the URL as-is to subscribe; lists update when the data changes and at least weekly. Format news news-lite hosts hosts/news.txt hosts/news-lite.txt domains domains/news.txt domains/news-lite.txt wildcard wildcard/news.txt wildcard/news-lite.txt adblock adblock/news.txt adblock/news-lite.txt dnsmasq dnsmasq/news.txt dnsmasq/news-lite.txt adblock, wildcard and dnsmasq entries block a domain and all its subdomains. Use one of these if your blocker supports it. hosts and domains list exact hostnames, because a hosts file can't match subdomains. Each site is expanded to the names people actually visit (www., m., amp., edition. and so on) using DNS checks. Pi-hole v6 (and v5 with FTL 5.22 or later) reads the adblock format and blocks subdomains; on older versions use lists/domains/news.txt. AdGuard Home · Filters → DNS blocklists → Add blocklist → Add a custom list → paste the adblock/news.txt URL. uBlock Origin · Dashboard → Filter lists → Import (at the bottom) → paste the adblock/news.txt URL → Apply changes. articles.fullContent: The 1985 SID sound · music and sound effects · 2 KB player, MIT The per-frame tricks of the classic C64 game music, in a grid you can see and edit while it plays. Make the sound effects with the same instruments, and drop music and effects into your own game: one call plays a laser over the tune. Open the tracker Play raster rumble “Hear it” plays 40 seconds of the raster rumble soundtrack, recorded from this tracker’s own engine: the real 6502 player on the reSIDfp chip emulation. Free, no account, no server. The Hubbard sound, with a grid Rob Hubbard’s music for Monty on the Run, Commando or Sanxion made three voices sound like a band. The secret was not in the notes but in his player, which changed the sound of the SID chip 50 times a second while a note was playing. Every one of those tricks is a field in the instrument editor here: Pulses that sweepThe pulse width moves while a note holds, so one note breathes instead of buzzing. Pulse width: sweep step, min, max Vibrato that comes in lateA note starts clean and only then begins to wobble, like a hand on a guitar string. Vibrato: delay, depth, speed Chords from one voiceOne voice runs through two or three notes so fast that you hear a chord. Arpeggio: offset, second offset Drums that share the bass channelA burst of noise and a falling tone make a kick or a snare, and the voice plays bass again on the next note. Drum: noise frames, fall Slides and divesLeads bend into notes, effects swoop down. Slide Small songsShort patterns, reused and transposed, make minutes of music out of a few hundred bytes. Order list: transpose per entry Sound effects, made like the music The laser, the jump and the explosion come from the same player as the tune. An effect is a short pattern for one voice, made in the Effects tab with the same instruments and the same editor. Your game starts it with one call, the effect borrows a voice for a moment, and the music on that voice comes back in time. Hear it in the Sound effects demo, or play raster rumble, which makes all of its sound this way. Why this did not exist before Hubbard wrote his music as numbers in his assembly source and played it with his own player. That player was never a tool anyone else could use, and its code is not free to copy. The trackers that came later show you the notes, but you have to build that per-frame sound yourself. Here the player was written from scratch around exactly those tricks, and the tracker runs that player: what you hear while you edit is what the exported files do on a real C64. What it is This project has two parts. The player is about 2 KB of 6502 assembly, written to be read in an afternoon. The tracker is a web page where you write songs for it. The page contains a 6502 core in JavaScript and the reSIDfp chip emulation, and it runs the real player code on them. Nothing is imitated: if it sounds right in the tracker, the same bytes sound right on the machine. How it started It began with a game. raster-rumble, a small C64 game, had a few hand-written sound effects and a simple tune, and they dragged it down. The classic players that sound right are not free to copy, and none of them came with a tracker where you can see the music while you write it. So both were built from scratch. raster-rumble now plays all of its sound through this player, and its music is a project you can open in the tracker. The player reads it and writes SID registers once per frame, exactly as it does on a C64. Those writes go to a chip emulation, and the result goes to your speakers. articles.fullContent: Local AI Tool Engine L.A.T.E. takes a local model (or an API model) and turns it into an agent. You give it a goal, and it works through it: it picks a tool, runs it, reads what came back, and keeps going until the job is done. Search the web, read pages and files, do exact maths, save files, remember things between chats. I built it because models on their own are bad at the boring parts. They get maths wrong, forget everything when the chat ends, and make things up instead of looking them up. Small models are worse: they skip steps, count letters in their head and lose track halfway through a job. So here the tools do the exact work, plain code handles the order of the steps, and the model mostly writes the answer. It runs with Ollama, LM Studio, or an API key (Groq, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Gemini, anything OpenAI-compatible). No LangChain, no paid API needed, two dependencies. What it does Exact answers. Maths, dates, unit conversion, counting, random numbers and weather come from real tools, not from the model's memory. Multi-step jobs. "Create a file, read it back, count the characters, save the count, read that file too" runs as exact steps, in order, and the answer lists what really happened. Works even when the model is tiny. Research with sources. It searches, opens the best pages, answers from what it read, and links them. Your files. Read a file, search a folder, copy, merge, sort the lines, change case, append text. Memory. Tell it something once, it remembers in later chats. forget really removes it. Saving files. Only after you say yes, and only into an ai-output folder. Terminal or browser. A terminal chat, or a small web page on your own computer. Rules first, model last. The plan for a job is made by plain code (the same words give the same plan every time). The model only writes text. A job is never answered with "here's how you could do it": it runs, or it says plainly that it couldn't. It says what really happened. The answer lists the steps that ran and what the tools returned. If a step failed it says "Partly done" or "I stopped at step N because...". If the last check found a difference it says "NOT a success". It never says "Done" for work that wasn't done. Getting started You need Node.js 18 or newer (I use 22). Then, in the project folder, one command: That's all. The first time it: installs what it needs (a minute, one time, you never type npm install), finds your model: Ollama or LM Studio if one is running (it can even download a small model for you), or you choose "API key" and pick OpenAI, Groq, OpenRouter, Gemini (or any OpenAI-compatible URL) and paste the key. It checks the key and lists the models, asks if you want PDF reading (adds one small library, about 1 MB), sends a test message, and opens the chat. After that, npm start just opens the chat. articles.fullContent: Your AI said it's done. Is it really done? Catch the AI code changes that pass your tests and are still wrong. AI coding agents say "done" when the tests pass. But the tests only check what somebody wrote down. Apex verify takes the change an AI made and the task you gave it, has a different AI write the missing checks, proves those checks can fail, runs them next to your own tests, and answers ready, not ready or unknown, with the evidence. It works on a copy of your code, so your project is never touched. It checks any change: the working tree an agent just edited, a branch, or a diff from any tool or person. It can also stand in the agent's way (a Claude Code and Gemini CLI hook that blocks "done") and gate pull requests (a GitHub Action). Why timing matters more than technique A tea brewing timer matters because tea keeps extracting as long as the leaves sit in water. A cup that tasted perfect at two minutes can turn harsh at ten. Time and temperature pull in opposite directions: hotter water extracts faster, so delicate teas need cooler water and a careful watch, while cooler water needs a longer steep to draw the flavour out. That is why the simplest habit in Chinese tea is also the most useful one: pour the tea out when the timer ends, and keep the leaves separate until the next infusion. If you do over-steep, the harshness comes from tannins released late in the extraction — don't throw the cup away, dilute it with a little hot water, or add a splash of milk for black tea. Cold brewing sits at the other end of the scale: leaves soak in cold water in the fridge for 6 to 12 hours, and the slow extraction keeps the bitterness down. Most Chinese teas can be steeped several times, and the second and third infusions are often the most interesting, because the leaves have fully opened. Add about 30 seconds for each later steep in a mug, or about 10 seconds in a small gongfu pot. Questions beginners ask How long should I steep green tea? About 2 minutes in water around 80°C. In a small gongfu pot, use more leaves and much shorter steeps: about 5 grams per 100 ml, starting at 20 to 45 seconds. Do I need a special timer? No. Any timer works. The point of this page is the numbers next to it: the right temperature and the right time for each kind of tea. Can I use this timer with tea bags? Yes, but shorten the time. Tea bags are filled with small broken leaves that release flavour fast — usually 1 to 2 minutes is enough, while whole loose leaves need 3 to 5. If the tea turns bitter, try 30 seconds less next time. Can I cold brew with this timer? Not really — cold brewing takes 6 to 12 hours in the fridge, so a minute timer is the wrong tool. Put the leaves in cold water, refrigerate, and taste after 6 hours. Green tea is usually ready sooner, black and oolong take longer. Strain and serve over ice.

With so many AI developer workflows now maintaining documentation, agent instruction and formal verification reporting in markdown, a great general purpose markdown reader is a useful tool to have. articles.title: How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO
articles.contentSnippet: Three significant backers share what gave them conviction to bet billions on Anthropic.
articles.fullContent: When Notable Capital poured roughly 10% of the U.S. portion of its $1 billion-plus fund into Anthropic’s Series E, many limited partners were perplexed by the massive bet. Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threatening to overtake closed-source competitors. Moreover, at $61.5 billion, Anthropic’s valuation was by far the highest that the predominantly early-stage venture firm had invested at in its 25-year history. But investors at Notable, formerly known as GGV Capital before its 2024 split from its China operations, were confident in Anthropic’s future. A team that included managing partners Hans Tung and Glenn Solomon and principal Dan Cahana crunched the numbers and found that developers were increasingly favoring Claude over ChatGPT, using Claude 70% of the time, a reversal from the previous year. “We just knew that for AI, the developer is at the center because they’re the early adopters,” Tung, a co-founder of the firm, told TechCrunch. Having navigated the complexities of U.S.-China relations firsthand, Notable was also convinced that “mission-critical” work would always require U.S.-based, closed-source models, Tung said. Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment. On Wednesday, Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times. Notable is, of course, not the only firm sitting on a massive paper windfall from Anthropic. Even traditional late-stage investors, who rarely see venture-scale multiples, are set for a big win. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC had been researching Anthropic throughout 2024, but it didn’t make its first investment until after Chris Emanuel, head of the fund’s tech investments, met with Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao at Che Fico, an Italian restaurant in San Francisco, in early 2025. Rao helped pique Emanuel’s interest in the company by showing that model improvements were driving rising enterprise adoption. GIC then made its first investment in Anthropic’s Series F, a round announced in September 2025 at a $183 billion valuation. “Claude Code was just released then,” Emanuel told TechCrunch. “It was very early, but even then, we could see signs that it was really popular with developers.” GIC’s conviction in the AI lab was so high that the fund later led Anthropic’s Series G alongside Coatue at a $380 billion valuation, and returned as one of the co-leads for the pre-IPO round at $965 billion. Across the three rounds, GIC invested more than $4.5 billion in Anthropic, amassing a stake equal to about 1% of the company after its IPO, according to a person familiar with GIC’s financials. Lilian Li, who leads U.S. growth investments at Baillie Gifford, began studying Anthropic and speaking with its team nearly two years before first investing in the company’s Series F. Baillie Gifford invested in the Claude maker once it became clear that the company was “executing consistently” on its vision while generating strong revenue and “compelling gross margins,” Li told TechCrunch. After Baillie Gifford’s initial investment, Anthropic continued to deliver on its promises, expanding into industries such as legal services and life sciences, as well as broader applications like Cowork and cybersecurity, Li said. “It’s actually quite incredible how consistent they have been with how quickly everything’s been changing,” she added. Baillie Gifford went on to invest a total of $1.5 billion across three funding rounds, a bet that has generated substantial paper gains for the investment manager, as well as for dozens of other backers who invested at what once seemed like astronomical valuations. articles.title: OpenAI’s chief scientist has thoughts on how to limit AI development
articles.contentSnippet: To establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how to measure speed.
articles.fullContent: A new blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity. Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.” But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name) could be that measurement. In Pachochki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.” Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5. “GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.” So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. articles.contentSnippet: Journalist Paris Marx unpacks his new book "Hyperscale."
articles.fullContent: In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine. The book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections. And those debates are likely to continue as Democrats wield more governmental power. In an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry. After all, if a data center is being built in your community, “it’s very physical, it’s very material.” “It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on,“ Marx said. “You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.” He also suggested that data center opposition is only the most visible piece of a wider movement targeting “the physical manifestations of the tech industry, […] whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.” During our conversation (which I’ve edited for length and clarity), Marx and I discussed data centers’ environmental impact, how tech companies are responding to community resistance, and what it’s actually like inside a data center. I liked your description of trying to get access to the inside of a “hyperscale” data center and then eventually taking a tour [of one]. Could you talk a little bit more about what that experience was like? How did you get in? What surprised you when you actually got in? Getting inside of a hyperscale data center was not the easiest task in the world. I spoke to some researchers who have been doing research on data centers for a number of years longer than I had, and they told me that before the generative AI moment, and before all the attention that has been put on data centers recently, that it was quite a bit easier to do so. I sent emails to a number of companies asking if I could get inside, often didn’t get a response, other times got a no. I ended up, after visiting the outsides of some data centers in places like northern Virginia and Ireland and spots like that, I actually went down to New Zealand to go inside of a data center itself. Obviously, you would expect that this is an infrastructure that is really securitized, because the data inside needs to be kept safe, obviously [they] have these big fences and all the security cameras around the data centers. But to go inside, I had to send my passport in advance. Then when I got there, they had to check the passport, and then as we were going through the data center itself, every single door in the data center was locked unless you had a key card to unlock it. articles.fullContent: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and, now more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. Waymo pulling its robotaxis off freeways (again) and Zoox robotaxis launching on the Uber app illustrate the push and pull between progress and setbacks in the autonomous vehicle industry. There are signs of growth. For instance, Tesla has now surpassed Waymo in Texas in the number of robotaxis registered with the state (Tesla has 1,507 and Waymo has 1,345). But does that translate to market dominance? A better metric, if we’re trying to gauge who is leading, would be commercial driverless miles. And if we’re measuring cost-efficiency, another useful metric would be driverless miles per vehicle. By those measures, Waymo is still ahead, based on data available to me. But with Waymo’s recent freeways setback and Tesla’s push to expand its robotaxi fleet with Cybercabs, that lead could shrink. Not that there needs to be a winner, by the way. Transportation is deeply fragmented, and there is room for multiple players in the U.S., not to mention the rest of the world. A/B test: humans vs. robots A recent discussion with my Autonocast co-host Ed Niedermeyer, whose book, “Elon Take the Wheel,” comes out December 1, got me thinking about how Las Vegas could soon become a real world A/B test of sorts for human-driven vs. autonomous ride-hailing services. Uber, as mentioned above, just added Zoox to its ride-hailing app in Las Vegas. For now, riders don’t have much of a choice. Uber customers can increase their chances of getting a Zoox robotaxi, and they can always decline a robot ride. But they can’t directly select a robotaxi. Instead, Uber riders will be matched with one if it’s available. Uber said that will soon change. The company plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in its app as “availability and reliability improve,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in November. Las Vegas will also become the first U.S. city where riders can access two fully driverless partners through the Uber app, he said. (Hyundai’s self-driving subsidiary Motional is also an Uber partner.) That would give Uber riders a meaningful choice: a human driver or a robotaxi, and potentially even which autonomous service to use. And it could offer a revealing look at what customers actually prefer when given that choice. Price could tip the balance, too. It makes me wonder whether Las Vegas will become the next battleground for organized labor as robotaxis begin competing directly with human drivers. articles.title: Can a TV be too large? An investigation
articles.contentSnippet: Can a TV be too large? This writer's recent upgrade to a 65-inch OLED came with some unexpected challenges.
articles.fullContent: For the past couple of years, I’ve wanted to upgrade my home entertainment situation from the humble trappings of my long sufficient 55-inch TCL smart TV to the model much coveted by cinephiles the world over: the OLED. The organic light-emitting diode is a specific monitor technology that has really changed the TV industry. Unlike an LED TV, which creates images by shining a backlight through a panel of pixels, OLEDs leverage millions of self-lighting pixels, which provides significantly better pixel control, and can generate a much more nuanced image with deeply vibrant colors and a more intense light and shadows. In short: They look way better. They are also significantly more expensive, which is one reason that I’ve held off on investing in one for years. However, this year I couldn’t wait any longer. I finally sprang for an upgrade and, since I was already upgrading on image quality, I decided to upgrade the size, too: I bought a 65-inch LG evo C4, which is the company’s mid-range unit released in 2024. At first, the experience was amazing. The television rendered colors and shadows wonderfully and, seeing as one of the goals with this purchase was to indulge my physical media habit, I began running through my collection of 4K Blu-ray discs with the madcap energy of a true fanatic. However, things took a bit of an unexpected turn when, midway through “McCabe and Mrs. Miller,” I was suddenly overcome by a wave of nausea. I’m not particularly sensitive to motion sickness, but this sensation — which made it feel vaguely like I was going to hurl — persisted for several hours after it initially began. It was then replaced by a small tension headache. In short: Not great. I discovered that this is actually a somewhat common experience for new OLED adopters. Indeed, Reddit is rife with posts from new television owners who claim they feel like their big new toy is breaking their brain. “I got the tv yesterday and still feel sick today,” one Redditor, who said they had recently purchased an LG C2, wrote. “Feel light headed and nauseous a day later. Thinking about taking it back. Is this normal? I’m scared to turn the thing on lol.” Others blamed the sheer size of the screen. One guy, who bought an 85-inch TLC, claimed it had led his wife to the conclusion that “it’s too big and say that she feels sick watching. Is that a thing that a screen can be too big?” There doesn’t seem to be a consensus on why this happens. Many Redditors blame certain motion-smoothing settings. However, my TV did not come with those settings enabled. Others blamed viewers for sitting too close to the screen — yet I was sitting a solid nine feet away, which is well within the recommended range for a 65-inch screen. Finally, others have argued that the screen brightness could be agitating users’ eyes. articles.fullContent: Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.Sheherazaad started making ripples in the music world a few years ago with her EP Qasr, which was produced by Grammy Award winner Arooj Aftab. Now she’s back with Khudgarzi, her reverb-drenched folk-noir debut LP that’s primarily sung in Urdu.The instrumentation on Khudgarzi draws on traditional South Asian music, including Carnatic and Hindustani styles, but also dabbles in Arabic folk traditions, as well as modern Western electronic music. Trip-hop flourishes and Spaghetti Western guitar brush up against tanbur and ghatam. Sheherazaad’s stunning voice sits atop dripping percussion and seasick drones singing about the plight of “The Selfish Woman.”For Sheherazaad, the character of the selfish woman isn’t the villain, it’s a charge leveled at women who didn’t conform to societal norms, “eccentric women whose desire for agency was often met with an awful end.” Even if you can’t understand most of the lyrics, the atmosphere tells the story clearly enough. From the barely simmering anger of “Registaan” to the bleak repetition of “Qatil” and the fantastical yearning of “Zeher,” Khudgarzi is clearly the work of a woman exploring what it means to be a woman, the lasting legacy of colonialism, and the perpetual threats of a patriarchal society.Khudgarzi is alternately a funeral dirge and a celebration of femininity. Sheherazaad owes a lot of the album’s ability to navigate these various themes and moods to her impressive production work, top-notch mixing by J. Valleau, and the cast of over 30 “genre-chaotic” virtuosic musicians including Ria Modak, Sarathy Korwar, Jay Chakravorty, Shunya, and Qasim Naqvi. The instrumentation never distracts, though. It’s not showy, and all emulsifies around Sheherazaad’s vocals in a shawl that feels equal parts comforting and oppressive.Khudgarzi is available now on Bandcamp and most major streaming platforms, including YouTube Music, Spotify, Apple Music, Deezer, and Qobuz.Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.Terrence O'Brien

articles.title: Tri-screen portable monitors aren’t for the faint of heart
articles.contentSnippet: Three extra screens boost multitasking but can distract and overwhelm.
articles.fullContent: I try to keep my workspaces uncluttered to minimize distractions. A tri-screen monitor makes it easier to manage multiple tasks simultaneously but doesn’t allow for the cleanest layout or setup, which presents its own challenges. It’s also worth noting that you need a decent amount of space to fully extend a triple-portable-monitor setup. The X90G measures about 46 inches across with the side panels flattened out. That’s wider than my desk. You’ll also need some clearance if you want to fold the side panels in toward the laptop more, perhaps for a closer view. Tri-portable monitors are geared toward people with minimal space who want the flexibility to carry three screens on the go. But these devices are bound to have some bulk. The X90G weighs 6.4 pounds, more than twice the weight of the Dell XPS ultralight laptop I tested it with. That’s a reasonable weight for three displays, but it still inevitably compromises portability. The monitor folded up with its handle and kickstand visible. Credit: Scharon Harding The monitor folded up with its handle and kickstand visible. Credit: Scharon Harding Alternatively, on days when I could leave the monitor set up and just plug in my laptop, it felt pretty magical to be instantly rewarded with three additional screens by plugging a USB-C cable into my PC. Sometimes less is more For someone seeking to maximize small spaces, a three-screen portable monitor sounds reasonable. In practice, though, it’s hard to strike the right balance between portability and screen space with this many displays. With devices like the X90G, you can quadruple the number of pixels at your disposal. But when I used the X90G, the screens all feel like separate entities, partially because one of them isn’t in line with the laptop’s screen at all. A triple portable monitor can’t moonlight as a larger, unified display, like some dual monitors can. A dual-screen portable monitor used as one unified display. Credit: Scharon Harding A dual-screen portable monitor used as one unified display. Credit: Scharon Harding That said, a tri-screen monitor can do things others can’t, including making it easier to share information with other people. But if you want a portable monitor for more traditional reasons, such as needing an easily transportable way to get more screen real estate, or if you prefer clear spaces for working, a triple monitor may be overkill, if not overwhelming.

articles.fullContent: This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology. The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some capabilities are improving exponentially—but models aren’t as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report updates METR’s widely shared time horizon plot, which tested models on a large suite of tasks. articles.fullContent: Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks. Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil. But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report. Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods. These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it, which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years. “There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.” How it works There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks. The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon. If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing.“Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans. ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations. But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.
